params.question: Which structure is responsible for secreting the mucus that makes up the bulk of normal, physiological vaginal discharge?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The columnar cells lining the endocervical canal secrete mucus under oestrogen and progesterone influence, and this forms the largest component of visible discharge, changing in volume and consistency across the cycle.
Not quite. These paired glands near the vaginal opening and urethra add only a small amount of lubricating mucus, mainly during arousal — they are not the major contributor to everyday discharge.
Not quite. Plasma leaking across capillaries in the vaginal mucosa under oestrogen adds a watery, serous component, but this is a minor contributor compared to endocervical mucus.
Not quite. Shed, glycogen-rich epithelial cells give the discharge its whitish appearance, but they are not the source of its bulk volume — that comes from endocervical mucus.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: of the four sources (endocervical glands, vaginal wall transudate, desquamated cells, Bartholin/Skene glands), the endocervical glands contribute the bulk of the visible mucous discharge.
Well done — recognising the endocervical glands as the main mucus source explains why discharge volume tracks oestrogen-driven cervical changes across the cycle.

interactions.label: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal dryness and irritation.

params.question: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal dryness and irritation. Her vaginal pH is 6.5, and wet mount shows very few lactobacilli. Which mechanism best explains this finding?

answers.text: Declining oestrogen reduces glycogen deposition in vaginal epithelial cells, so lactobacilli have less substrate to ferment into lactic acid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Oestrogen drives glycogen deposition in the vaginal epithelium; without it, lactobacilli lose their substrate, lactic acid production falls, and pH rises toward neutral — the same mechanism that keeps pre-pubertal girls' pH near 6–7.

answers.text: Postmenopausal women develop bacterial vaginosis at higher rates for reasons unrelated to vaginal pH

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. The finding here is explained directly by the oestrogen-glycogen-lactobacillus axis, not by an unrelated predisposition to bacterial vaginosis.

answers.text: Reduced oestrogen causes excessive douching behaviour, which strips the acidic environment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Douching is a separate, behavioural disruptor of the vaginal ecosystem — it is not caused by low oestrogen, and nothing in this vignette suggests douching.

answers.text: Menstrual blood exposure has alkalinised the vaginal environment permanently

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Menstrual blood transiently raises pH during a period, but this patient is postmenopausal and no longer menstruates — the sustained rise here is due to oestrogen loss, not blood exposure.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the chain: oestrogen → glycogen deposition → lactobacillus fermentation → lactic acid → acidic pH. When oestrogen falls, as at menopause, every downstream step weakens and pH rises toward neutral.

Exactly — break the oestrogen link at either end of reproductive life (pre-puberty or menopause) and the same glycogen-lactobacillus-lactic acid chain fails, raising vaginal pH and predisposing to atrophic changes or infection.

params.question: A woman reports a profuse, frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge with an unpleasant odour and pain during intercourse. On speculum examination, you note tiny punctate haemorrhages on the cervical surface. Which diagnosis best fits this picture?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Frothy, yellow-green discharge with dyspareunia and a 'strawberry cervix' (punctate cervical haemorrhages) is the classic presentation of Trichomonas vaginalis infection.
Not quite. Bacterial vaginosis produces a thin, grey-white discharge with a fishy odour and typically no itching or soreness — it does not cause frothy discharge or a strawberry cervix.
Not quite. Candidiasis causes thick, white, curd-like discharge with intense itching and vulval redness, without the frothy quality or strawberry cervix seen here.
Not quite. Physiological discharge is clear to whitish, odourless, and non-irritating — the malodour, frothiness, and cervical haemorrhages here all point to an infective cause.

overallFeedback.feedback: Match the pattern: no itch with fishy odour suggests bacterial vaginosis; intense itch with normal pH suggests candidiasis; frothy discharge with a strawberry cervix and raised pH points to trichomoniasis.
Right — frothy yellow-green discharge plus a strawberry cervix is a specific enough combination to suspect trichomoniasis on clinical grounds alone.

interactions.label: On a saline wet mount prepared promptly at the bedside, which finding is most sp

params.question: On a saline wet mount prepared promptly at the bedside, which finding is most specific for trichomoniasis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Trichomonas vaginalis appears as motile, flagellated organisms on a fresh wet mount; the motility fades within minutes, so the slide must be examined promptly.

answers.text: Clue cells with minimal white blood cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Clue cells (epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria) with few white cells are the signature of bacterial vaginosis, not trichomoniasis.
Not quite. Pseudohyphae with abundant white cells indicate vulvovaginal candidiasis, not trichomoniasis.

answers.text: Numerous lactobacilli with rare white blood cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not quite. Abundant lactobacilli with few white cells is the expected picture in a healthy, normal wet mount, not an infected one.

overallFeedback.feedback: Each organism has its own wet mount signature: clue cells for bacterial vaginosis, pseudohyphae for candidiasis, and motile flagellated organisms — best seen fresh — for trichomoniasis.
Correct — motile flagellates are the key diagnostic clue for trichomoniasis, but they must be looked for quickly since motility is lost soon after the sample is taken.

interactions.label: Partner treatment is mandatory for bacterial vaginosis, in the same way that it

params.question: Partner treatment is mandatory for bacterial vaginosis, in the same way that it is for trichomoniasis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is actually false. Bacterial vaginosis reflects an imbalance of the woman's own vaginal flora rather than a sexually transmitted infection, so routine partner treatment is not needed — unlike trichomoniasis, where partner treatment is mandatory to prevent reinfection.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct, this statement is false. Bacterial vaginosis is a disruption of normal vaginal flora, not a sexually transmitted infection, so partner treatment is not routinely required. Trichomoniasis, in contrast, is a true STI where partner treatment is mandatory to prevent near-certain reinfection.
